item.title: On Reaction Depth and Fast Fault-Tolerant Boolean Logic
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — Any Boolean arithmetic circuit compiles to quantum circuits with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth using homogeneous Z- and X-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs) plus Toffoli states, at exponential space cost with dirty ancillas.

Grade 0.469 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Christopher Kang, Alexander Cowtan, Adam Bene Watts, Guillaume Dauphinais, Benjamin Ide

Asks

How can reaction depth be formalized and minimized for coherent fault-tolerant Boolean logic?

But

Requires exponential space overhead and leaves ancilla qubits dirty; relies on supply of clean Toffoli states.

Tools

reaction depth formalization · homogeneous Pauli Product Measurements · Toffoli state injection · AutoAND circuits

Abstract

Reducing runtimes of quantum applications is critical for practical viability. On quantum computers, the runtime can depend both on the speed of quantum operations and on how often the program must wait for the classical coprocessor to determine adaptive operations. Some recent approaches to reducing this overhead have focused on minimizing the "reaction depth" of a computation, informally defined as the number of times the classical coprocessor must be consulted while running a quantum program. In this work, we formalize the notion of reaction depth. We find several subtleties in this theory. For example, we distinguish the reaction depth of a circuit from that of a circuit run, and show that the magic depth of a unitary can be higher than the reaction depth once compiled into Clifford computation and magic state injection. We then focus on the specific case of coherent Boolean logic, a common and expensive component in quantum algorithms. We use a natural gateset for fast operations with Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes, which consists of homogeneous Z- and X-type Pauli Product Measurements (PPMs), alongside a supply of Toffoli states. We prove that, using this gateset, any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented on a quantum computer with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth, at the cost of exponential space and leaving some qubits "dirty". Using the same gateset we find two efficient AutoAND circuits that require only a Toffoli state and homogeneous PPMs. We then give efficient implementations of the quantum ripple-carry adder and quantum schoolbook multiplier, which require a low number of heterogeneous PPMs for uncomputation. We find implementations competitive with the state-of-the-art despite the restricted gateset.

item.title: Quantum Parallel Algorithm for Multivariate Trace Estimation with Applications
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Parallel quantum algorithm estimates multivariate traces Tr(A1A2…Ak) with circuit depth independent of k, scaling with qubit count Θ(k) and distributable across 𝒪(k) devices.

Grade 0.401 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Algorithm for Linear Systems of Equations” · Honghong Lin, Yun Shang

Asks

Can multivariate traces Tr(A1A2…Ak) be estimated on near-term quantum devices with circuit depth independent of k?

But

Requires access to matrices via vectorized state preparation oracles; qubit overhead scales as Θ(k).

Tools

matrix vectorization · tensor network representations · parallel quantum circuits · distributed quantum computing

Abstract

Estimating multivariate traces Tr(A1A2......Ak) is a fundamental task arising across diverse fields. In this paper, We develop a quantum algorithm for this problem tailored to near-term quantum devices. We access matrices by preparing their vectorized states. This access mode yields a tensor-network representation of the multivariate trace, which in turn guides the design of a parallel algorithm. The resulting circuit has depth dominated solely by that of the input oracle and independent of the number of matrices k, at the cost of a qubit count scaling as Θ(k)-a trade-off between circuit depth and circuit size. Moreover, the circuit exhibits a simple modular structure that allows explicit distribution over O(k) devices. We further establish efficient preparation circuits for a broad range of matrix classes, demonstrating the wide applicability of our approach. we present two applications: spectral sum estimation and a quantum implementation of the classical Lanczos method. Both reduce the target problem to sums of multivariate traces, thereby avoiding the construction of matrix polynomial transformations and achieving two levels of parallelism. For certain matrix classes, the resulting algorithms reduce circuit depth by a factor equal to the degree of the approximating polynomial. The shallow circuit depth and distributed implementation make our algorithms particularly suitable for near-term devices.

item.title: Optimal Joint Bounds for Sparse Ground-State Energy Estimation and Ground-State Preparation
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Sparse-query complexities of guided ground-state energy estimation and preparation scale as Θ(slog⁡(1/ε)/(γδ)) and Θ(slog⁡(1/ε)/(γΔ)), respectively, settling the optimal joint parameter dependence.

Grade 0.399 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Hamiltonian Simulation by Qubitization” · Dhrumil Patel

Asks

How does the quantum query complexity of guided ground-state energy estimation and ground-state preparation depend jointly on sparsity s, overlap γ, precision δ or gap Δ, and error probability ε in the sparse-access model?

Before

Optimal bounds in time-evolution and block-encoding models were Θ(log⁡(1/ε)/(γδ)) and Θ(log⁡(1/ε)/(γΔ)) (Jeffery & Witteveen 2026; Jeffery, Somma, Witteveen & de Wolf 2026; Somma & de Wolf 2026), leaving sparsity dependence open.

But

Lower bounds allow degenerate ground spaces and rely on stoquastic Hamiltonians without geometric locality; upper bounds require reversible in-place sparse-location oracles.

Tools

Boolean query reduction (position-parity) · reversible in-place sparse-location oracles · exact Cayley transduction · quantum eigenvalue transformation

Abstract

Ground-state energy estimation (GSEE) and ground-state preparation (GSP) are fundamental problems in quantum computing. Given a Hamiltonian H with |H|≤1 and a guiding state |ψ⟩ with overlap at least γ>0 with the ground space of H, the goal in GSEE is to estimate the ground-state energy of H to additive error δ with failure probability at most ε, while in GSP it is to prepare a state with ground-space weight at least 1-ε, given a gap lower bound Δ. Their costs are measured by quantum query complexity, i.e., the number of oracle calls needed to access H. Recent work proved optimal bounds Θ(log(1/ε)/(γδ)) for GSEE and Θ(log(1/ε)/(γΔ)) for GSP in the time-evolution and block-encoding models. However, these models do not directly account for the sparsity of H, measured by the maximum number s of nonzero entries in any row or column. In the sparse-access model, oracles instead return the locations and values of these entries. This introduces the additional parameter s, and it remained open how query complexity depends jointly on s, γ, δ or Δ, and ε. We resolve this by proving sparse-query lower bounds Ω(√slog(1/ε)/(γδ)) for GSEE and Ω(√slog(1/ε)/(γΔ)) for GSP, even for stoquastic Hamiltonians. We also show that these constructions recover the earlier time-evolution and block-encoding lower-bound scalings. We then give matching upper-bound algorithms in the reversible in-place sparse-location model. Thus, we obtain Θ(√slog(1/ε)/(γδ)) for GSEE and Θ(√slog(1/ε)/(γΔ)) for GSP, showing that √s is necessary and sufficient and completing the joint dependence on all problem parameters.

item.title: Efficient simulation of variational quantum circuits: representation, accuracy and CPU/GPU allocation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Direct Pauli evolution via NumPy accelerates two-layer full LiH variational evaluations 3.45-fold over elementary-gate simulation, whereas an RTX PRO 6000 GPU yields roughly 30-fold speedup over an 18-thread Aer CPU baseline for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM in FP64.

Grade 0.396 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Vojtvech Novák, Radovan Revcka, Ondvrej Knebl, Ivan Zelinka

Figure

Per-call latency of four-layer spin VHA in FP64 versus qubit count, comparing elementary gate decomposition, direct Pauli updates, specialized commuting-block updates, and single-GPU acceleration across thread counts.

Asks

How should simulation representation, precision, and CPU/GPU resource allocation be jointly chosen to minimize the cost of repeated variational quantum circuit energy evaluations under accuracy and hardware constraints?

But

Evaluations assume fixed-parameter scalar energy calls, not full optimizer convergence trajectories; unobserved vectors outside candidate comparison subsets are not certified; MPS requires low entanglement.

Tools

Qiskit Aer and Statevector · Pennylane Lightning direct Pauli evolution · CUDA-Q GPU adapter · Matrix product states (MPS) · NumPy state updates

Abstract

Classical circuit simulation supports quantum software development and verification and provides a baseline for assessing quantum advantage. We compare gate-based statevector simulation, direct Pauli evolution and matrix product states for molecular and spin Variational Hamiltonian Ansatze and hardware-efficient ansatze on CPU/GPU systems, varying width, depth, precision and resource allocation. In the tested implementations, direct Pauli evolution benefits complex molecular VHA, whereas GPUs accelerate wider spin and hardware efficient circuits. Matrix product state is useful when limited entanglement permits accurate compression; corrected CPU FP32 can meet the tested tolerance while costing more than FP64. Workload size, startup, worker memory and task-specific profiling can change the preferred allocation. Matched NumPy Pauli updates accelerate two-layer full LiH by 3.45-fold; the GPU gives approximately 30-fold acceleration over 18-thread Aer for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM, both in FP64. We provide a procedure for choosing representation, precision and worker allocation jointly, comparing the cost of complete energy evaluations under accuracy, memory and core constraints.

item.title: A provably efficient classical algorithm for simulating OTOC⁽¹⁾ in 1D
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Window propagation computes first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits at arbitrary depth in classical polynomial time with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error ε=1/poly(n). On 512-qubit Clifford circuits with 768 T-gates, mean-squared error drops from 1.97×10−2 to 1.31×10−4 as window width increases from 2log2⁡n to 5log2⁡n.

Grade 0.390 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Laura Lewis, Antonio A. Mele, Ronald de Wolf, Jarrod R. McClean, Amira Abbas

Figure

OTOC values per circuit instance and mean squared error against window width w for 80 Clifford+T circuit instances at n∈{128,256,512} qubits.

Asks

Are out-of-time-order correlators classically hard to simulate?

But

Applies strictly to first-order OTOCs in 1D; does not apply to second-order OTOCs in 2D.

Tools

window propagation algorithm · Haar-random brickwork circuits · Clifford+T circuits · two-copy operator space truncation

Abstract

Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are quantities of broad interest in many-body physics due to their connection with information scrambling and quantum chaos. Recently, estimating higher-order OTOCs in random quantum circuits was proposed as a promising avenue for quantum advantage, yet the classical hardness of this task remains poorly understood. Even for first-order OTOCs, where growing evidence suggests classical tractability, no efficient classical algorithm with rigorous guarantees has been established to date. In this work, we introduce "window propagation," the first provably polynomial-time classical algorithm for approximating first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits, at arbitrary depths and with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error. We also conduct numerical experiments comparing our simulation results to exact computation on up to 512 qubits for Clifford circuits with 768 T-gates and up to 22 qubits for Haar-random circuits. We emphasize that our results do not directly apply to second-order OTOCs in 2D, which is the subject of recent quantum advantage proposals. Nevertheless, our work provides a rigorous step towards understanding the classical complexity of OTOC estimation and represents a family of non-trivial quantum circuits for which a provable, polynomial time algorithm is now known, establishing foundations for understanding these widely used diagnostics of quantum chaos.

item.title: Quantum Annealing with a Quantum Neural Network: Width of Annealing Matters
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Expanding quantum annealing to width W=2 in a random quantum neural network exponentially reduces required depth Lmin under linear annealing for unstructured search. A tuned quantum perceptron of depth L=1 and width W=2 solves the search problem with exponentially small error.

Grade 0.389 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “A variational eigenvalue solver on a photonic quantum processor” · Mojtaba Asadollahi, Danial Khajehzadeh, Abolfazl Ramezanpour

Figure

Minimal annealing depth Lmin(δ) versus system size N for unstructured search at threshold δ=1/3. Linear schedule depth drops exponentially from W=1 to W=2,3, while Grover schedule performance is unchanged by width.

Asks

Can broadening the width of a quantum annealing process through a quantum neural network architecture improve annealing efficiency across quantum phase transitions?

Before

Standard quantum annealing on unstructured search requires minimal depth scaling as Lmin∝2N with linear schedule, or Lmin(G)∝2N via Grover schedule.

But

Complexity scales exponentially with network depth as WL; state reconstruction success probability falls as 1/WL for orthogonal states; tested on small qubit counts or via mean-field factorized product states (N=400).

Tools

quantum neural network · linear annealing schedule · exact numerical simulation · mean-field Hamiltonian approximation · differential evolution

Abstract

Quantum annealing is a promising quantum algorithm for dealing with computationally hard optimization problems. Currently available hardware can implement the algorithm for a significant class of Hamiltonian problems. However, its performance is especially limited in discontinuous quantum phase transitions, where the energy gap shrinks exponentially with system size. In this paper, we introduce an extension of quantum annealing to a quantum neural network and study its performance in a number of prototypical optimization problems. In particular, we observe that already a random quantum annealing network of width W = 2 can exponentially reduce the number of evolution layers or depth of the annealing process in the quantum search problem. By tuning the network parameters the search problem can be solved with exponentially small errors by a quantum perceptron of depth L = 1 and width W = 2. The findings show that width of a quantum annealing network is critical to enhance the success probability of the algorithm by providing a larger and learnable evolution space for the annealing process.
